prerequisites.meaning: A unit of text processed or generated by a language model.
prerequisites.check: Are character count and token count always the same?
prerequisites.answer: No. A token can be a whole word, part of a word or punctuation.

prerequisites.meaning: A named piece of code taking inputs and returning an output.
prerequisites.check: What are the inputs and output of a chat response function?
prerequisites.answer: Inputs: the messages and settings such as max_tokens. Output: the generated reply.

prerequisites.meaning: A structured text format for exchanging named fields and values.
prerequisites.check: In {"max_tokens":64}, which part is the field name?
prerequisites.answer: max_tokens is the field name; 64 is its value.

prerequisites.meaning: An interface through which one program asks another to do work.
prerequisites.check: Does a browser need the provider's secret key?
prerequisites.answer: No. The secret key stays on the server; the browser talks to your server.

prerequisites.meaning: The time a request waits for a result.
prerequisites.check: Is first-token wait the same as full-answer wait?
prerequisites.answer: No. The first token usually arrives well before the full answer is finished.

diagrams.title: A monitored chat application
diagrams.subtitle: Follow the actual Gradio path through the lab's respond function
trace: A student types a question in the Gradio interface.
respond checks the current message before calling the local model.
An allowed message reaches generate; a blocked request skips model generation.
The output is checked and a metadata-only JSON log line is written.
Monitoring aggregates allowed-request latency and all-request block counts.
diagrams.explanation: Deployment turns a model into a system that accepts requests and returns usable answers. In this lab, Gradio calls the Python respond function directly. The separate FastAPI exercise offers another route to the same model; the Gradio interface does not call that API. The respond function first applies an input check to the current message. Allowed requests combine a system instruction, recent history and cleaned text, then generate returns answer text and token counts. A basic output check runs before the answer is returned. Blocked requests skip generation and receive a refusal. Both paths write latency, model identity, token counts and the blocking reason to a JSON-lines log. Monitoring summarises those records into percentiles and counts. These simple pattern checks illustrate the flow; they do not guarantee that every injection or personal-data format will be detected.
diagrams.check_question: Does a blocked request consume model-generation tokens in respond?
diagrams.check_answer: No. It skips generate and logs zero prompt and completion token counts for that request.

diagrams.title: From API request to generated answer
diagrams.subtitle: The endpoint translates structured messages into tokens and back
trace: The SDK sends 'Name two uses of FastAPI.' to the local endpoint.
ChatRequest parses messages and max_tokens; the endpoint caps output length.
generate formats messages into tokens and waits for the shared model lock.
Only generated continuation tokens are decoded as the assistant answer.
The response includes choices and a usage block for the SDK to read.
diagrams.explanation: An API is an interface through which one program requests work from another. The OpenAI-compatible exercise receives an HTTP request containing JSON fields. FastAPI uses ChatRequest to parse the body, and chat_completions passes its messages to generate. The chat template adds the role markers expected by the model, while the tokenizer converts the formatted text to token IDs. MODEL_LOCK prevents the notebook and server from generating on the shared model simultaneously. The model's output includes the original input prefix plus its continuation. The generate function slices away that prefix, decodes only new tokens and reports input and output counts. The endpoint packages those results into choices and usage fields. Compatibility concerns this response structure; the lab endpoint remains a small demonstration without the authentication, streaming or complete request controls of a deployed service.
diagrams.check_question: Why are prompt and completion token counts returned separately?
diagrams.check_answer: They describe different work: reading the input and producing the answer. They support usage and cost calculations.

diagrams.title: Measure before deploying
diagrams.subtitle: Connect speed, cost, quality and application logs
trace: Compare first non-empty text time with full-answer time in lat_df.
Inspect the local API answer and its usage counts.
Compare weight approximation error with perplexity after fake quantisation.
Observe batching throughput separately from single-request latency.
Inspect which simulated requests were blocked or redacted and compare p50 with p95.
diagrams.explanation: The lab begins with streaming measurements before introducing serving. The measure function times the first non-empty decoded text chunk, an approximation of first-token latency because a chunk can contain several tokens. The FastAPI exercise then exposes generation to a client program. The monthly_cost function uses classroom prices, while retry simulation illustrates delayed retries after rate limiting. The efficiency experiments distinguish different tradeoffs: fake_quantize approximates low-bit weights but restores them as floating-point tensors, so the size table is theoretical; batching measures aggregate throughput; caching reuses an answer for a repeated message list. The Gradio application calls respond directly, adding simple checks and log records. Finally, synthetic traffic produces a monitoring summary. The generated Docker files are a smaller packaging scaffold, so compare their features with the notebook before assuming equivalent application behaviour.
diagrams.check_question: Does fake_quantize reduce the actual model tensor storage to four bits in this experiment?
diagrams.check_answer: No. It rounds then dequantises weights into floating-point tensors. The size estimate describes hypothetical packed low-bit storage.

diagrams.title: Prepare a model for a measured release
diagrams.subtitle: Deployment changes the running system; it does not train weights
diagrams.insert_before_title: Packaging and releasing: Docker, versions, CI
diagrams.explanation: Deployment prepares an existing model for use through an application. First record its identity, prompt and generation settings. Measure task quality and speed before making efficiency changes, so later differences have a baseline. The lab illustrates weight rounding, batching and response caching; fake_quantize is a simulation with floating-point tensors, not a genuine low-bit serving engine. Packaging records the environment and start command. The exported app scaffold is smaller than the notebook handler, so inspect which checks it includes. Monitoring a limited trial checks whether real request timing and failures match expectations. None of these steps trains the model weights; they change how the application operates.
trace: Record the selected model name before measuring a fixed question set.
A cache can make a repeated request fast; also measure uncached requests.
Check task answers after an efficiency change.
Inspect the packaging scaffold and compare it with the checked notebook handler.
diagrams.check_question: Does a theoretical 4-bit size table show that this notebook stores weights in 4-bit tensors?
diagrams.check_answer: No. fake_quantize rounds values but keeps floating-point tensors; the storage estimate is theoretical.

diagrams.title: Follow allowed and blocked app requests
diagrams.subtitle: Gradio calls respond directly; the FastAPI route is separate
diagrams.explanation: The checked Gradio route begins in respond. It tests the current message for a small set of patterns and may block it or redact matching personal information. If allowed, it builds messages from the cleaned request and recent history, calls generate, then checks the answer. It records metadata such as timing, token counts and block reason without storing raw prompts in this handler's log. A blocked input skips generation but still creates a log record. These rules are examples: they can miss different personal-data forms and attacks. In particular, checking the current message alone does not clean all earlier history. The separate FastAPI exercise does not automatically inherit respond's checks or logging.
trace: A permitted request reaches generation and records input/output token counts.
A blocked current message receives a refusal without running the model.
Both paths add a metadata row that monitoring can count.
Inspect earlier history too; a clean newest message does not make old content safe.
diagrams.check_question: If the API endpoint uses generate directly, does it inherit respond's input checks?
diagrams.check_answer: No. Controls must be applied on each reachable request route.

glossary.meaning: A URL and request handler through which a program exposes an operation.
The elapsed time needed to serve a request.
Work completed per unit time, such as total generated tokens per second.
Time to first token; this lab approximates it with first non-empty decoded text.
Representing weights with a limited set of values, often to store fewer bits.
Processing several inputs together in one model operation.
Stored results reused when an equivalent request returns.
A latency value at or below which roughly 95% of measured requests fall.

pitfalls: Higher batching throughput does not automatically mean lower latency for every individual user.
The notebook's fake quantisation size estimates do not describe actual packed tensor memory.
The Gradio path and FastAPI path are separate exercises; input checks in respond do not protect the API endpoint.

recap.example: 500 students → expected requests → token/GPU cost → load test → checked interface → monitoring.
recap.question: Batching doubles throughput. Must each student receive an answer sooner?
recap.answer: No. More total tokens per second can coexist with a longer wait for one request.
recap.next: In Week 12 we add retrieved evidence and controlled tool use.
recap.notes: Return to the 500-student warm-up. Ask students to identify the model, server, interface and monitoring responsibilities. Distinguish the first visible text from the complete response, then use the exit question to separate throughput from individual waiting time. Revisit the illustrative bill: input and output tokens have separate rates. Explain that fake quantisation measures approximation error while keeping floating-point tensors. Follow one allowed and one blocked request through respond. The Gradio route uses that handler, while the separate API route calls generate directly. Finish by asking what must be tested before using the smaller Docker scaffold as a real application.
